newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Santer to face Euro-MPs' anger on BSE.
newsitem.headline: Santer to face Euro-MPs' anger on BSE.

text.p: The European Parliament is set this week to condemn the European Commission for serious errors in the mad cow crisis but is likely to give President Jacques Santer time to put matters right before imposing sanctions.

The Parliament, often dismissed as a talking shop, has used new powers given it by the Maastricht Treaty to investigate what went wrong during the mad cow crisis and is determined that this time its warnings are heeded.

A scathing report by a special committee of inquiry attacked Britain for failing to enforce eradication measures, Brussels for giving protection of the beef market priority over public health and both for negligence and minimising the risks.

On Tuesday in a crucial debate in Strasbourg, the affable Santer will have to pledge further tough measures to prevent any recurrence of the public health scare caused by the spread of the fatal brain diseases, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

A shake-up last week of the EU's food safety services, which were stripped from the powerful farm commissioner Franz Fischler and put under the control of the popular consumer affairs chief, Emma Bonino, has not satisfied the Parliament.

Many Euro MPs have demanded that EU officials responsible for making mistakes should be sacked or given other duties and that legal action should be brought against Britain, which they hold mainly responsible for the crisis.

Britain's failure in March 1996 to forewarn its EU partners that BSE could be transmitted to humans shattered consumer confidence and undermined the beef market. BSE started in Britain and has mainly hit British herds.

But a legal move against either British farm minister Douglas Hogg for failing to appear before the committee of inquiry, or against the British government for damages caused by the BSE crisis, would have to be initiated by the Commission.

Despite widespread dissatisfaction, a censure motion on Thursday by maverick Belgian socialist Jose Happart urging the immediate dismissal of Santer and his 19 commissioners stands virtually no chance of success, parliamentary officials said.
It is highly unlikely to gain the necessary backing of two- thirds of the votes cast and an absolute majority of 314 votes in the assembly.

Even Happart's 214-member Socialist Group, the largest in the assembly, has dismissed the move as an "ill-judged" fringe attempt that risked plunging the EU into a crisis that would serve no-one's interests.
"The top priority is protection of consumer health and making sure that we never have another scandal like mad cow disease again," Socialist leader Pauline Green said in a statement.
Green said that Santer must first have an opportunity to act upon the recommendations of the report.
There were only three socialists among the 63 signatories needed to force Happart's censure vote.

The Parliament's second main political group, the Christian Democrats, is also against seeking the immediate dismissal of the Commission, whose Luxembourger president belongs to the same political camp.

Many Euro MPs also feel it would be unfair to make Santer and his team, which entered office in January 1995, the scapegoat when the most serious sins and omissions were committed during President Jacques Delors term of office.

Depending on Santer's performance in Tuesday's debate, the two main political groups, supported by the Greens, are likely to back a compromise under which the Commission would be put on "probation," officials said.

After the Parliament on Wednesday adopts the committee's report, a motion would be presented, probably in March, under which Santer would be given until December to take corrective measures against BSE or face a censure vote for dismissal.
